issues.legal_issue: A borrower’s writ petition challenging secured-loan recovery should ordinarily not be entertained when an effective statutory remedy is available, unless a recognized exception to the alternative-remedy rule is established.
material_facts: The borrower filed a writ petition after the creditor rejected objections to the proposed recovery action, seeking regularisation of the loan account and alleging a violation of natural justice without giving supporting particulars or identifying prejudice.
By the time the interim order was made, the creditor had taken the further recovery action that made a statutory tribunal remedy available.
The writ petition did not explain why that remedy was ineffective or give compelling reasons for bypassing it; the asserted inability to repay was attributed to the borrower’s own circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition because an effective statutory remedy was available and no recognized exception was established.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, a writ petition should ordinarily not be entertained where an effective alternative remedy exists, particularly where a statute supplies a comprehensive recovery process and a forum for redress. Recognized exceptions include action contrary to the governing enactment, defiance of fundamental judicial procedure, reliance on repealed provisions, or total violation of natural justice. Under Sections 13(4) and 17 of the SARFAESI Act, an aggrieved person may challenge the secured creditor’s recovery action before the Debt Recovery Tribunal; the explanation to Section 17 provides that the communication rejecting a representation or objection at the earlier Section 13(3A) stage does not itself entitle the borrower to apply to the Tribunal. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income Tax v. Chhabil Dass Agarwal, United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tandon, General Manager, Sri Siddeshwara Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. Ikbal, Punjab National Bank v. O.C. Krishnan, Kanaiyalal Lalchand Sachdev v. State of Maharashtra, and other authorities applying the alternative-remedy rule.

rule.if: borrower_recovery_writ and statutory_tribunal_remedy_available and not recognized_exception_established

predicates.borrower_recovery_writ: A borrower has brought a writ petition challenging a secured creditor’s loan-recovery action.
predicates.statutory_tribunal_remedy_available: A statutory tribunal remedy is available to challenge the creditor’s recovery action.
predicates.recognized_exception_established: The borrower has established facts bringing the case within a recognized exception to the ordinary rule against writ relief when an effective alternative remedy exists.

issues.definition: When a borrower challenges secured-loan recovery by writ, an available tribunal remedy and the absence of an established exception mean the writ should not be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: An interim stay of secured-creditor recovery is unsustainable when granted ex parte without special reasons and without giving the creditor an opportunity to contest the petition’s maintainability.
material_facts: The High Court, on the first date and without giving the creditor an opportunity to file a reply, stayed further recovery proceedings on condition that the borrower make a deposit.
The interim order did not give special reasons for granting relief or address the available statutory remedy.
The creditor’s recovery action concerned public funds, and the stay impeded recovery.
issues.conclusion: The interim stay was granted without adequate justification and could not be sustained; the High Court should not have granted it on the circumstances presented.
issues.legal_principle: In matters involving recovery of public dues and secured loans, the High Court must exercise its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 226 with particular caution because an effective statutory remedy is generally available and a stay may adversely affect financial institutions and the public interest. Any departure from the ordinary rule must rest on reasons showing that a defined exception applies, with the relevant law and circumstances considered. The Court relied on United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tandon, Union Bank of India v. Panchanan Subudhi, General Manager, Sri Siddeshwara Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. Ikbal, and the principles in Baburam Prakash Chandra Maheshwari v. Antarim Zila Parishad, Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, and Harbanslal Sahnia v. Indian Oil Corporation.

rule.if: secured_creditor_recovery_case and ex_parte_interim_stay_granted and not special_reasons_recorded and creditor_given_no_opportunity_to_oppose

predicates.secured_creditor_recovery_case: The proceeding concerns a secured creditor’s recovery of a loan.
predicates.ex_parte_interim_stay_granted: The court grants an interim stay without first hearing the creditor.
predicates.special_reasons_recorded: The court records special reasons supporting the stay after considering whether a recognized exception justifies departure from the ordinary rule.
predicates.creditor_given_no_opportunity_to_oppose: The creditor is given an opportunity to oppose the petition or the request for interim relief before the stay is granted.

issues.definition: In secured-creditor recovery proceedings, an ex parte stay without recorded special reasons and an opportunity for the creditor to oppose it is unsustainable.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may intervene under Article 136 against an interim order in special circumstances to prevent manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process.
material_facts: The appeal challenged an interim order in a pending writ proceeding and the appellate order declining to interfere with it.
The interim order departed from settled law on the availability of a statutory remedy, was made without hearing the creditor, and stayed recovery without special reasons.
The High Court’s approach was contrary to settled decisions of the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: Special circumstances justified interference, and the challenged orders were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court is ordinarily reluctant to interfere under Article 136 with an interim order in a pending proceeding, but may do so in special circumstances to prevent manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process. The Court also relied on Dwarikesh Sugar Industries Ltd. v. Prem Heavy Engineering Works (P) Ltd. for the principle that subordinate courts should not disregard settled law or grant relief contrary to it.

predicates.appeal_from_interim_order: The appeal asks the Supreme Court to review an interim order made in a pending proceeding.
predicates.order_contrary_to_settled_law: The challenged order departs from settled legal principles applicable to the dispute.
predicates.manifest_injustice_or_abuse_risk: The circumstances show a risk of manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process if the order is left undisturbed.

issues.definition: On an appeal from an interim order, departure from settled law creating a risk of manifest injustice or abuse warrants Supreme Court intervention.
